content:
The charge runs like this: Muhammad (peace be upon him) silenced his critics by having them killed at night. The list usually carries four names: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Abu Rafi' ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and the poets Asma bint Marwan and Abu Afak.

Two of those killings are in Sahih al-Bukhari, and this page concedes them and reads them in their setting. The other two rest on reports the hadith critics reject. The difference matters, because the case is usually pressed hardest on the weakest pair.

The report is sound and it is blunt. Jabir ibn Abd Allah relates that the Prophet asked, "Who is willing to kill Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who has hurt Allah and His Apostle?" Muhammad ibn Maslama offered, asked leave to "say a thing" to Ka'b, meaning words that would draw him out, and was told he might. He and his companions went to Ka'b at night, talked him out of his house and killed him (Bukhari 4037; Muslim 1801).[1]

So it was a planned killing, and it used a ruse. Any honest answer starts there. The question is what Ka'b had done. Ka'b was a leader among the Jews of Medina through his mother's tribe, the Banu Nadir. After the battle of Badr, Ibn Ishaq reports, he rode to Mecca, mourned the Quraysh dead in verse and urged them to take revenge on Medina, then came home and wrote verses about Muslim women.[2] The Medina agreement that bound the city's tribes forbade giving protection to Quraysh or to anyone who helped them.[2] By the terms he had agreed to, a man who went to the enemy and called for war on his own city had gone over to the enemy.

I will not soften what the jurists did with the case, though. Ibn Taymiyya made the killing of Ka'b a central proof, in al-Sarim al-maslul, for his ruling that a non-Muslim under covenant who reviles the Prophet has broken the covenant.[3] That is a ruling of law, argued from this report, and a reader is entitled to weigh it. What the report itself records is a man who was helping an army that had just fought Medina and would fight it again.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib relates that the Prophet sent a party of the Ansar under Abd Allah ibn Atik to Abu Rafi', "who used to hurt Allah's Apostle and help his enemies", and that Abd Allah entered his fortress at night and killed him (Bukhari 4039).[4]

Abu Rafi' ibn Abi al-Huqayq was a leader of the Banu Nadir, who had been sent out of Medina and settled at Khaybar. Ibn Ishaq names him among the men who went round the tribes and raised the confederate army that besieged Medina at the Trench in 627.[5] Killing the organiser of an army that has already marched on your city is an act of war. A reader may still dislike how it was done. The report does not show a critic killed for his words.

This is the story most often quoted: a woman who mocked the Prophet in verse, killed at night by Umayr ibn Adi while her child lay at her breast. It is told in Ibn Sa'd's Tabaqat, from al-Waqidi, and in a version with a chain back to Ibn Abbas.[6]

Both chains fail. The Ibn Abbas version runs through Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj al-Lakhmi. Al-Bukhari said his hadith is to be rejected, Ibn Ma'in called him a liar, and Ibn Adi said that this is the man who fabricated the hadith of the woman who used to lampoon the Messenger of God. Ibn al-Jawzi placed the report in his collection of fabrications, and al-Albani graded it fabricated in al-Silsila al-da'ifa, number 6013.[6] The other version comes from al-Waqidi, whom Ahmad ibn Hanbal called a liar and al-Bukhari and Abu Hatim listed as abandoned.[6]

So the story fails the test the Muslim scholars themselves apply to every report about the Prophet. A critic who cites it is citing a report those scholars threw out.

Abu Afak is said to have been an old man of the Banu Amr ibn Awf who wrote verses against the Prophet and was killed in his sleep by Salim ibn Umayr. Ibn Ishaq tells the story with no chain of transmission at all. Al-Waqidi tells it with chains, and Ibn Sa'd takes it from him, so every chain runs through al-Waqidi.[7]

A report with no chain cannot be checked, and a report that rests on al-Waqidi alone does not meet the standard for a claim about what the Prophet ordered. The honest verdict is that the story is not established. That is a weaker claim than proving it false, and I will not dress it up as more. It means a case against the Prophet cannot rest on it.

The bottom line

Two men were killed on the Prophet's order, and the sound reports say so plainly: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who went to Mecca after Badr to call Quraysh to war, and Abu Rafi', who helped raise the army that besieged Medina. Both acts belong to a war that was being fought, against men who were fighting it.

The two poets are another matter. The story of Asma bint Marwan comes through a narrator named as its forger, and the story of Abu Afak has no chain that holds. Judge the Prophet on the first two if you must. The second two are not evidence.

Notes

  1. Sahih al-Bukhari 4037 (Book of Military Expeditions), the report of Jabir ibn Abd Allah; Sahih Muslim 1801 (Book of Jihad and Expeditions).
  2. Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-nabawiyya (the recension of Ibn Ishaq), the killing of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and the text of the agreement between the Muslims and the Jews of Medina, with its clause that Quraysh and those who help them are given no protection.
  3. Ibn Taymiyya, al-Sarim al-maslul ala shatim al-rasul, the discussion of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 4039 (Book of Military Expeditions), the report of al-Bara' ibn Azib.
  5. Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-nabawiyya, the battle of the Trench, on the men of the Banu Nadir who raised the confederates.
  6. Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-kubra, the expedition of Umayr ibn Adi; Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Mawdu'at, vol. 3, p. 18, quoting Ibn Adi on Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj; al-Dhahabi, Mizan al-i'tidal, vol. 3, p. 509 (Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj) and vol. 3, p. 663 (al-Waqidi); Ibn Hajar, Tahdhib al-tahdhib, vol. 9, p. 163 (al-Waqidi); al-Albani, Silsilat al-ahadith al-da'ifa wa-l-mawdu'a, no. 6013.
  7. Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-nabawiyya, the killing of Abu Afak, given without a chain; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-kubra, the expedition of Salim ibn Umayr, from al-Waqidi.
